The most common win left on "50X The Cash" is $10. The second biggest prize left is $50,000, and one of those are still unclaimed. The prize table is what defines a scratcher, and this page counts every level of it.

The table below shows the full count for "50X The Cash", with every prize level included.
981.headline: What the prize table shows

985.body:
"MAX-A-MILLION" can match another game on price and top prize and still pay out very differently. This game is a game built around small prizes that are won often. Of its unclaimed prize money, most is in wins under $5,000 and the rest is in bigger prizes. Neither kind is better, and each suits different players.

Everything above about "MAX-A-MILLION" comes from the North Carolina Lottery's own published numbers. We only do the counting.
985.headline: Where the prize money is

988.body:
The prize money on "Emerald 10's" leans toward many smaller prizes. It is spread over eleven prize levels, from wins equal to the ticket price up to $1 million. Games built like this give out wins often, but rarely large ones. That design never changes, and it is the part you choose.

Every line of Emerald 10's's prize table below shows today's count, not last month's.
988.headline: Where the prize money is

990.body:
About three-quarters of the tickets for "LADY LUCK" are sold. The top prize count has held, with two of four still unclaimed. The number of tickets printed is fixed, so that is a plain good sign.

Everything here about "LADY LUCK" comes from official North Carolina lottery numbers, current through November 1.
990.headline: Good news: no big claims

992.body:
The top prize count on "$2 MILLION VAULT" has not moved since we started watching it. The game still has one of three top prizes unclaimed. Smaller prizes keep getting claimed as tickets sell. The same top prizes are now among fewer tickets.

Tomorrow's count on "$2 MILLION VAULT" will be a little different. The game sells every day, and this page keeps track.
992.headline: No new top prize claims

993.body:
"$5,000 Triple Play" has gone five months without a top prize claim, and tickets kept selling. Only a fixed number of tickets are printed. About three-quarters of the tickets are sold, and every remaining $5,000 prize is still unclaimed. That leaves the same top prizes among fewer tickets.

Tomorrow's count on "$5,000 Triple Play" will be a little different. The game sells every day, and this page keeps track.
993.headline: Good news: no big claims

994.body:
"$25,000 Triple Play" offers a top prize of $25,000 and twelve prize levels in all. The prize money leans toward many smaller prizes. Games shaped like this pay small prizes often and large prizes rarely. This design never changes, while every other number on this page does.

The table below shows the full count for "$25,000 Triple Play", with every prize level included.
994.headline: Same price, different prizes

995.body:
The top prize count on "$200,000 Triple Play" has not moved since we started watching it. The game still has two of four top prizes unclaimed. Smaller prizes keep getting claimed as tickets sell. The same top prizes are now among fewer tickets.

If "$200,000 Triple Play" is your usual pick, check this page often. The prize counts change even when the ticket looks the same.
995.headline: Tickets sell, top prizes remain

996.body:
"$1,000,000 Triple Play" is past the halfway point of its run, with about a third of its tickets still unsold. Late in a run, a game is worth a look when prizes outlast tickets. Early on, the prize design matters most. Here, a larger share of the top prizes is left than of the tickets, which is a good sign.

Every line of $1,000,000 Triple Play's prize table below shows today's count, not last month's.
996.headline: Early stage or late
